name: Menelik II
info: Menelik II, baptised Sahle Maryam, was king of Shewa from 1866 and Emperor of Ethiopia from 1889 to 1913; he expanded the empire to its greatest extent, defeated Italian forces at Adwa in 1896 and began the modernisation of the state.

facts.born: 19 August 1844 (or 17 August) in Ankober, Shewa, as Sahle Maryam; son of Haile Melekot, Negus of Shewa, and Ejigayehu; of the Shewan branch of the Solomonic dynasty
facts.died: 12 December 1913 (also placed in the night of 12 to 13 December), after strokes from 1906; buried in a mausoleum at the Menelik Palace in Addis Ababa
facts.role: King (Negus) of Shewa from 1866 to 1889, quasi-independent from 1878; Emperor of Ethiopia from 1889 until his death in 1913
facts.known: the defeat of Italy at the Battle of Adwa in 1896; the southern conquests that took the Ethiopian Empire to its greatest extent; the Treaty of Wuchale and its two versions; the Addis Ababa to Djibouti railway; a cabinet of ministers, schools and a state bank; the atrocities and enslavement associated with the annexations

t: Held at Tewodros II's fortress of Maqdala from boyhood, Menelik escaped in 1865, took the kingdom of Shewa in 1866 and after the death of Yohannes IV was crowned emperor on 3 November 1889.

His southern conquests, financed partly by ivory, coffee, gold and a taxed slave trade, brought the Oromo, Wolayta, Gurage and other peoples into the empire, and at Adwa on 1 March 1896 his army defeated Italian colonial forces.

He is regarded as the architect of modern Ethiopia and as a symbol of African resistance to colonialism, while critics among the incorporated peoples, notably the Oromo, accuse him of atrocities, land expropriation and forced assimilation.
dyk: Menelik was named after the legendary Menelik I, son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, by his grandfather Sahle Selassie, who is said to have prophesied a reign in which the Ethiopian Empire would be reconstituted.
ev: Sahle Maryam, later Menelik II, is born at Ankober in the kingdom of Shewa
After fighting between Tewodros II and his father's Shewans, the boy is captured and taken to Tewodros's court at Maqdala
Menelik escapes from Maqdala, and in 1866 proclaims himself Negus of Shewa
By the Treaty of Wadara he submits to Emperor Yohannes IV with a stone round his neck and is crowned Negus of Shewa with the Emperor's consent
Shewan forces defeat the emir of Harar at Chelenqo and Harar is annexed
After the death of Yohannes IV he is crowned emperor on Mount Entoto on 3 November
He defeats Italian forces at the Battle of Adwa and Italy recognises Ethiopia's independence by the Treaty of Addis Ababa
Menelik dies after years of paralysis

sections.early:
Menelik was born as Sahle Maryam on 19 August 1844 in Ankober, in the kingdom of Shewa, the son of Haile Melekot, Negus of Shewa, and Ejigayehu, said to have been a young woman working for the sovereign's mother Bezabish. His grandfather Sahle Selassie named the child Menelik, after the legendary Menelik I. Haile Melekot at first refused to acknowledge him, but Bezabish had him legitimised by a council of relatives; another version holds that Haile Melekot briefly married the mother. His tutor was Ato Nadew, who stayed close to him all his life.

In October 1855 fighting broke out between the forces of Emperor Tewodros II and those of Haile Melekot. The Negus ordered Debre Berhan evacuated and burned, and had loyal Shewan chiefs, among them Darge Sahle Selassie, take Menelik to the Minjar plateau. Darge submitted in February 1856, Tewodros annexed Shewa, and Menelik was taken to the emperor's palace at Maqdala.

There he was received as a prince. Menelik later said that Tewodros had treated him like a son and told him more than once that he would reign after him. His education was provided by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, and he studied military strategy and horsemanship. Tewodros made him a Dejazmach and gave him his daughter Altash in marriage in 1864. He was probably influenced by Tewodros's policies of unification and centralisation.
sections.rise:
As Tewodros's authority declined, Menelik escaped from Maqdala on the night of 1 July 1865, aged 21. Tewodros then ordered the execution of the imprisoned son of Queen Worqitu of Wello, who had hoped to exchange Menelik for him. Tewodros's punitive expedition of early 1866 killed mainly civilians, and he ordered the sacking of Gondar in November 1866 and a massacre of 800 soldiers around mid-1867; these acts led many soldiers to join Menelik. In August 1866 he reached eastern Shewa and proclaimed himself Negus. At the Battle of Qewet most of the soldiers of the rival Ato Bezabeh joined him, and Bezabeh, first pardoned, was later tried for conspiring with the Oromo and shot.

In letters of 1867 he called himself King of Kings, but he did not help the British expedition of 1868 against Tewodros, who took his own life. Menelik's imperial ambitions were checked by Yohannes IV, crowned emperor in 1872. After Yohannes defeated the Egyptians at Gundet and Gura, Menelik's hopes of replacing him ended. A rebellion in Shewa in 1877, linked to his wife Bafena, further weakened him. In 1878 Yohannes marched on Shewa and, by the Treaty of Wadara of 20 March, Menelik submitted with a stone round his neck and renounced the imperial title, receiving part of Wello and the Emperor's consent to be crowned Negus of Shewa.
sections.deeds:
Confined to Shewa, Menelik turned south. Between 1879 and 1884 his forces moved along the Rift Valley against the Hadiya, Kambata, Silte and Welayta, and he defeated Negus Tekle Haimanot of Gojjam at Embabo in 1882. Ras Gobana Dache occupied Wollega in 1886, when Menelik moved his capital to Addis Ababa, and on 6 January 1887 Harar was annexed after the defeat of Emir Abd Allah at Chelenqo. Ivory, musk, coffee and gold were exported, and Menelik also benefited from a slave trade conducted by Muslim entrepreneurs but taxed by the Shewan state; the arms bought with these revenues enabled further conquests. Administration was based on garrison towns (katamas) built to house the neftenya. The Swiss engineer Alfred Ilg, who arrived in 1879, became his chief European adviser.

On 2 May 1889 Menelik signed the Treaty of Wuchale with Italy. The Italian version gave Italy more power than the Amharic, and Menelik rejected the treaty on learning of it. In 1895 he called out the nobility, and his army defeated Italian forces at Amba Alagi, took Mekele, and on 1 March 1896 won at Adwa. By the Treaty of Addis Ababa Italy recognised Ethiopia's independence. Conquests continued to 1900, reaching Lake Rudolf. Modernisation followed: the Menelik thaler of 1894, a postal system, schools, the Bank of Abyssinia (1905), the railway from Djibouti and, in 1907, a cabinet of ministers.
sections.opponents:
Menelik's opponents within the empire included Ato Bezabeh, Negus Tekle Haimanot of Gojjam and, for years, Emperor Yohannes IV. His wife Bafena was implicated in a plot against him in Shewa, and he divorced her in 1882. He sought to be conciliatory toward enemies, and an edict in Shewa forbade religious debate and allowed all religions.

The expansion was resisted by the peoples it absorbed. The Arsi yielded only in 1886, and the kingdom of Kaffa at first refused tribute before being conquered. The campaigns that began in 1894 followed the great famine Kifou Qen, caused by rinderpest, which killed over 90 per cent of the cattle. Menelik and his wife Taytu Betul are reported to have owned 70,000 slaves.

His legacy is contested because of the atrocities committed by his army against civilians and combatants during the annexations, which many historians consider to constitute genocide. Awol Allo wrote that Menelik, who masterminded the victory at Adwa, also presided over some of the most brutal atrocities against groups in the south, particularly the Oromo, and that for Oromos he is "devil incarnate". Critics among the incorporated peoples have also accused him of forced assimilation, land expropriation and cultural suppression, which they say contributed to later ethnic tensions.
sections.last:
In mid-1906 Menelik suffered a massive stroke and was seriously ill by January 1907. Fearing the empire might collapse, Britain, France and Italy signed a Tripartite Treaty in December 1906 to divide it between themselves in that event. The cabinet of 1907 was intended to answer the same fear. A second stroke came in May 1908 and a third in April 1909 left him paralysed and barely able to speak.

The succession was followed closely by his wife Taytu, who wished to shift power towards Gondar and her Yejju family. At the proclamation of the will on 18 May 1909 his grandson Iyasu was named heir presumptive, but Taytu had the will changed so that the heir was named only as Lij ("my child"), which left unclear whether Iyasu or Menelik's daughter Zewditu was meant. On 30 October 1909 the Council of Ministers proclaimed the will with Iyasu's name and appointed Ras Bitwoded Tessema Nadew regent. Power remained in Taytu's hands until veterans of the army confronted her in March 1910 and she agreed to stay with Menelik without involving herself in politics. Tessema Nadew held power until he died on 10 April 1911.

From 1910 to 1913 Menelik's death was announced several times in error. He died on 12 December 1913 and was buried in a mausoleum at the Menelik Palace in Addis Ababa. Iyasu nominally succeeded him but was never crowned and was deposed by nobles in 1916 in favour of Zewditu, with Ras Tafari Makonnen as regent and heir.
sections.legacy:
Menelik is generally considered the founder of modern Ethiopia. His borders, set by treaties with Britain, France and Italy, his ministries, schools, bank and railway, and the extension of the empire to its greatest historical extent shaped the state that followed him. His successors came from his own family: his grandson Iyasu, his daughter Zewditu, and Ras Tafari Makonnen, the future Haile Selassie.

Adwa gave him an international reputation. He was praised as a symbol of African resistance to colonialism, and the Adwa Victory Day is celebrated every March in Ethiopia; the victory is also said to have inspired Pan-African movements around the world. A Serb legend, recounted by the anthropologist Mary E. Durham, made Menelik a kinsman of the Montenegrin royal house on the strength of a similarity of names.

The other side of his memory comes from the peoples of the south. Allo writes that the Oromo are ambivalent toward Adwa because of its association with Menelik. He was a controversial figure for much of his reign.

summary: Menelik II (1844–1913) escaped from captivity under Tewodros II, became king of Shewa in 1866 and emperor in 1889. His southern conquests extended the empire, his army defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896, and critics among the Oromo and others charge him with atrocities.
notes: Birth date: the opening says 17 August 1844, the Early life section 19 August 1844. Both given in facts.born; 19 August used in the text.
Death: opening gives 12 December 1913; Decline section says the night of 12 to 13 December. Both stated.
Capture at Maqdala: the lede says he was imprisoned at 11 after his father's death in 1855; the body says he was 12 when captured after February 1856. No age is given in the text. Event dated 1856.

Treaty of Wuchale: the lede says Menelik formally rejected it in 1891; the body gives no year. The lede says the Italian version 'implied a protectorate'; the body says it 'gave Italy more power'. The body is followed. The lede also says it was signed 1889 and body 2 May 1889. The Wuchale section includes a muddled paragraph about Italian help to become King of Abyssinia and Eritrea, left out. Article cites Article 17 only in the Italo-Ethiopian War section without stating its content.

Bafena: the divorce is given as 1882 (Wives section), but the section also says she was married 1865 'for seventeen years'. The Shewa rebellion is dated 1877 in the text but the imprisonment of Meshesha 14 December 1876 is given in the same paragraph; the sequence is muddled and left out. Her plot is told as allegedly instigated by her.

Taytu: one passage says Emperor Yohannes was able to broaden his power base through Taytu's family connections, which is probably an error for Menelik. Left out. 'Went to the Battle of Adwa with 5,000 troops' also left out.
Abba Jifar II slaves passage and its statement that the practice was common 'for thousands of years' left out.

Battle of Adwa: the article gives no figures, casualties or tactics for the battle itself, and its lede mentions an army of over 100,000. The deeds section therefore says only that he won. Italian force details at Amba Alagi (2,150 men, 1,000 killed) left out for space.
Famine: the article says the 1894 campaigns aimed to address the famine Kifou Qen; this is stated as the article's reading ('followed' used in the text).
Embabo date: 6 or 7 June 1882 in the article; only the year used. 'Moved his capital to Addis Ababa' is in the Wollega sentence, 1886.
Statement in 'opponents' that Menelik 'was said to be conciliatory': the article says he sought to be conciliatory from the start; edict wording attributed to the Shewan edict.

Genocide claim: the article says it is considered by many historians as constituting genocide; Awol Allo quoted at length. Critics' list (forced assimilation, land expropriation, cultural suppression) is the lede's; the lede attributes it to critics among incorporated ethnic groups.

Left out: the Tripartite-era list of wives' relatives, the three natural children and their genealogy (partly contradictory: Zewditu's age at marriage, Abeto Asfa Wossen), the Rimbaud and other European visitors, the electric chair link, and the 2 million rounds bribe.
References: left empty for the editor.
